title: Dendritic spines observed by extracellular DiI dye and immunolabeling under confocal microscopy
protocol: Anesthetize the rat with ketamine and xylazine (80 and 10 mg/kg, intraperitoneally).
Inject heparin (1000 IU) into the left ventricle.
Perform transcardiac perfusion with a peristaltic pump using 0.9% saline solution followed by 1.5% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 20 to 30 minutes.
Remove the brain carefully from the skull, avoiding damage to the duramater and arachnoid.
Transfer the brain to a small vial containing the fixative solution and immerse it for 1 hour.
Transfer the brain to 0.1 M PBS, pH 7.4.
Place the brain on a tissue culture dish with PBS.
Trim a block of the brain enclosing the area to be studied.
Glue the trimmed brain block onto the tissue holder using Super Bonder, Crazy Glue, or similar adhesive.
Fill the vibratome chamber with PBS immediately after gluing.
Dry the base of the tissue block quickly before gluing.
Maintain the vibratome chamber surrounded by ice for lightly-fixed tissue to help with sectioning.
Place a half double-edged razor blade in the vibratome at an angle of approximately 45 degrees inclined down and forward.
Select a high magnitude of vibration, e.g., 8-10 on the Leica vibratome.
Set a slow speed for the razor advancement, e.g., 1-2.
Slice the brain with an appropriate thickness to obtain a representative sample of the intended area.
Collect slices in PBS on glass slides.
Avoid drying tissues during collection.
Place sonicated fine powdered DiI gently over a bundle of axons or their proximity using a thin histological needle or glass micropipette with a sharp tip.
Remove large crumbs of crystals for better diffusion.
Place DiI in an Eppendorf tube for sonication.
Sonicate the DiI for at least 10 hours before use.
Remove a small sample of sonicated DiI and visually evaluate it.
Ensure that sonicated DiI crystals have turned into a very fine pink powder, thin enough not to be individualized by the naked eye.
Apply powdered DiI over the tissue using a dissecting microscope.
Use 1-10 μg of powdered DiI for generating good results (no need to weigh, just use a tiny amount on the tip of a needle).
Determine the appropriate amount of DiI for each experiment through pilot tests.
Place powdered DiI dye over a known axonal efferent pathway from the studied areas.
Keep the exposed tissue sections on glass slides covered with PBS at room temperature (around 22°C) for approximately 16 hours in the dark.
Remove the 0.1 M PBS and proceed to the final fixation of the tissue with 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 30 min.
Rinse the fixative solution with 0.1 M PBS.
Counterstain with DAPI (0.13 ml DAPI in 6.25 ml PBS) for 3 minutes.
Wash the slices with PBS twice, each for 10 minutes.
Mount the slices under coverslip using anti-fading non-diluted mounting media (Fluoromount, VectaShield or similar).
Avoid air bubbles during mounting.
Seal the borders of the coverslip with a fast drying nail polish to prevent the mounting media from drying.
Maintain the slides under refrigeration for no more than 7 days until confocal microscope visualization.
Encircle the sections on the glass with a hydrophobic pen (PAP pen, EMS, cat no. 71310).
Prepare a solution of 0.2% Tween in 0.02M TBS.
Incubate sections with the 0.2% Tween-TBS solution for 6 hours at 4°C.
Block sections with 2% BSA and 0.1% Tween in 0.02M TBS for 1 hour at room temperature.
Incubate sections overnight at 4°C with polyclonal primary antibody rabbit anti-synaptophisin diluted 1:100 in 0.5% BSA and 0.1% Tween in TBS.
Wash the tissue twice for 10 minutes each with 0.5% BSA and 0.1% Tween in TBS.
Incubate sections with appropriate secondary antibodies diluted in 0.5% BSA and 0.1% Tween in TBS for 2 hours at 4°C.
Wash slides with TBS twice for 10 minutes each.
Place sonicated powdered DiI on the slides as previously described.
Keep the slides in a humid chamber at 40°C for 48 hours.
Wash slides with water twice for 10 minutes each.
Obtain images using a Leica SP5 confocal microscope.
Use a plan-apochromat 40x oil-immersion lens for imaging.
Adjust spectral detectors to capture emission from Helium/Neon laser at 558 to 637 nm wavelengths for DiI.
Set pinhole diameter to Airy 1.
Acquire Z-stack with step intervals of 0.15 to 0.3 µm.
Set frame size resolution to 4096 × 4096 pixels.
Represent voxel size as 55.6 × 55.6 × 299.9 nm.
Set image acquire range to 8 bits.
Use undiluted anti-fading mounting media generously over sections.
Avoid excessive over or undersaturated pixels during imaging.
Add channels with different secondary antibodies for visualizing other proteins.
Reconstruct dendrites of interest by adding z-stack images using Leica Microsystems LAS AF Lite software.
Enlarge 3D images to determine spine shape and quantity along dendrites.
Resolve spine type or number slowly moving back and forth through the "z" stacks.
Classify spines as stubby, thin, mushroom-like, filopodium-like, ramified, or with a gemule aspect based on morphology.
Differentiate spine types by examining length of stalk, head shape, and number of protusions from a single stalk.
Divide the number of spines per unit length of dendrites imaged in 3D using Lite software.
Use NeurolucidaR from Microbrightfield, USA, to obtain 3D measures of dendritic branches.
Use Image Pro-Plus 7.0 basic pack to get linear measure of a dendritic branch.
Calculate the dendritic 3D length by multiplying the sum of stacks with the step size.
Consider DiI labeled spines and pre-synaptic synaptophysin immunolabeling in contact when their pixels are in the same focal plane without background.
Consider DiI labeled spines and pre-synaptic synaptophysin immunolabeling in contact if there is overlapping between yellow DiI pixels and red puncta of synaptophysin in at least one focal plane.
Visualize dendritic spines close to a synaptophysin-labeled terminal to determine the number of spines establishing a synaptic contact.
Ensure that synaptophysin labeling occurs without harming DiI labeling, penetrating 10 to 15 µm from the section surface.
Observe synaptophysin labeling on synaptic contacts on dendritic shafts and spines, on the stalk, top, or laterally to the head and neck of the spines.
